disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation) is characterized by a persistent pattern of developmentally inappropriate inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity that causes clinically significant impairment across settings (e.g., work, home, social). In adults, it often presents as disorganization, difficulty sustaining focus, restlessness, and impulsive decision-making rather than overt hyperactivity seen in children. Symptoms must have been present since childhood, but many individuals only come to clinical attention in adulthood when environmental demands exceed their compensatory strategies. It is differentiated from mood, anxiety, and personality disorders by its early onset, chronic course, and cross-situational pattern of attentional and impulse-control difficulties, and it commonly co-occurs with anxiety, depression, and substance use disorders.

narrative.personality: Kevin is a structured, introverted, and analytical counselor who prefers predictable routines, quiet hobbies, and methodical problem-solving.
narrative.stressor: Kevin had always relied on rigid routines and meticulous checklists to get through school and earlier jobs, but as he transitioned into a more complex counseling role while simultaneously starting his LPC supervision and part-time master’s coursework, the sheer volume of tasks and deadlines increased dramatically. The demands of managing a growing caseload, coordinating community outreach events, and keeping up with readings and assignments for graduate classes began to outstrip the informal systems he had used to stay on top of things. Over the next year and a half, he noticed that despite spending long hours at his desk, he was missing practical follow-through on everyday responsibilities like returning calls, handling small administrative tasks, and keeping track of household errands, which led to awkward moments with clients, supervisors, and his spouse. The mounting professional embarrassment, subtle feedback from his clinical supervisor about reliability, and tension at home about dropped responsibilities finally prompted him to seek a psychiatric evaluation when he realized his usual strategies and self-discipline were no longer enough.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep forgetting everyday things—calls, small tasks, errands—and it’s starting to cause problems at work and at home.”

narrative.personality: Clara is a disciplined yet eclectic professional who channels her creativity into structured planning, aesthetics, and an active, socially engaged lifestyle.
narrative.stressor: About two years ago, Clara was promoted from a project-focused engineering role into a senior community association manager position, which shifted her work from discrete technical tasks to constant coordination among residents, boards, vendors, and retrofit projects. The new role required her to sit through long board meetings, attend back-to-back negotiations, and spend more time behind a desk planning multi-year budgets and upgrades, sharply contrasting with her previously mobile, hands-on work style. As her responsibilities expanded, she found it increasingly difficult to tolerate the prolonged periods of sitting still in formal settings and the unrelenting stream of competing demands, so she began overloading her off-hours with yoga, hikes, concerts, and travel in an effort to “burn off” a persistent internal agitation. When even these outlets stopped feeling sufficient and she noticed that her constant urge to be on the move was affecting her concentration in high-stakes meetings and her ability to unwind at home, she sought psychiatric help to understand why she felt so perpetually keyed up despite outward career success.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I can’t ever sit still or relax, especially in meetings, like I’m always wound up and restless.”

narrative.personality: Calvin is a quiet, methodical planner who enjoys solitary, detail-oriented hobbies and approaches work with analytical precision and frugality.
narrative.stressor: Calvin’s promotion to lead event and recreation program manager for a large multi-site operation in Greater Boston brought a sharp increase in complexity: overlapping event timelines, intricate contracts, and multi-layered reporting requirements. Historically, he had masked lifelong attention difficulties by working alone, taking extra time, and double- and triple-checking his work, but the new role demanded rapid turnarounds, delegation, and simultaneous oversight of numerous details he could no longer personally micromanage. Over the following 1 year and 10 months, small oversights in proposals, logistical plans, and budget spreadsheets began to accumulate, leading to near-misses with venue bookings, errors in invoices, and uncomfortable questions from leadership about reliability, which deeply conflicted with his self-image as meticulous and exacting. As his anxiety about making mistakes grew and he found himself spending excessive hours trying—but failing—to prevent further slip-ups, he became increasingly distressed and finally agreed to a psychiatric evaluation after a trusted colleague gently suggested that his ongoing struggles with detail-oriented tasks might reflect an underlying attention issue rather than a temporary stress reaction.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I keep making small, avoidable mistakes in my event plans and budgets, even when I’m trying my hardest to be careful.”
